analysis.one_liner: Lets the Treasury clarify which workers count as employees for tax purposes and cracks down on misclassifying employees as contractors.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, vote, or any action beyond its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1978, a law has barred the Treasury Department from writing rules about whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor for tax purposes. This bill repealed that ban, directed Treasury to issue clear rules, and required businesses that regularly hire contractors to tell them in writing which tax and labor protections they do not have. It also raised penalties for businesses with no honest reason for treating workers as contractors, while shielding businesses that had a reasonable basis from retroactive tax bills.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers treated as contractors when they function as employees. Misclassification means no payroll taxes paid on their behalf, no unemployment insurance, and often no health, retirement, or workplace-safety protections [S2]. Businesses that classify workers correctly would also benefit, since rivals who misclassify save on payroll taxes and gain an unfair price advantage [S2]. The Treasury would collect more of the roughly hundreds of billions in taxes lost to misreporting each year [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Lifts the 1978 ban that stops Treasury from issuing rules or guidance clarifying whether workers are employees or independent contractors for employment tax purposes, and directs the Secretary to issue such guidance [S2][S3].

Requires businesses that regularly use independent contractors to give them written notice of their federal tax obligations, the labor and employment law protections that do not apply to them, and their right to ask the IRS for a status determination [S2][S3].

Eliminates reduced penalties for failing to withhold income taxes where the taxpayer has no reasonable basis for treating a worker as a contractor, and tightens the standard after an IRS final determination to clear and convincing evidence [S2][S3].
Protects businesses with a reasonable basis for contractor treatment from retroactive employment tax assessments dating back to 1978, easing the transition to new rules [S2][S3].
Requires annual Treasury reports on worker misclassification enforcement and new statistically valid data on how many workers and employers are affected and the cost to the tax gap [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that rely on treating employees as independent contractors to avoid payroll taxes, unemployment insurance, and benefits would face reclassification, back taxes where they lacked a reasonable basis, and full penalties. Some of that cost could show up as higher prices or fewer contract arrangements. Workers shifted to employee status would see take-home payroll tax withholding but gain employer-paid taxes and benefits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Businesses using contractor classification to cut labor costs

drawbacks.text: The bill does not itself define when a worker is an employee; it authorizes Treasury to write the rules, which creates a period of regulatory uncertainty for small businesses as new guidance takes effect a year after enactment [S3].

Businesses that relied in good faith on past IRS audits, industry practice, or prior rulings are protected from retroactive liability, but firms that fail the reasonable-basis test face full penalties and back employment taxes, raising compliance costs that could be passed to consumers or reduce contracting work [S3].

The bill includes a special carve-out for securities broker-dealers: compliance instructions imposed only under investor-protection rules cannot be weighed in deciding whether a broker is an employee, making it easier to treat brokers as contractors and applying retroactively to services after December 31, 1997 [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill addresses a real, decades-old problem: because Treasury has been banned since 1978 from clarifying worker classification, employees mislabeled as contractors lose unemployment insurance, benefits, and workplace protections, and honest employers subsidize rivals who cut costs through misclassification [S2]. The bill is carefully built — reasonable-basis protection from retroactive assessments, a one-year transition, burden-of-proof rules for cooperative taxpayers — so the main downside is transition uncertainty for small businesses. The securities broker-dealer carve-out, which weakens employee status for a specific financial industry and applies retroactively, is a poorly fitting special interest provision inside an otherwise worker-focused bill.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced it and sent it to the Finance Committee in November 2013, and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced S. 1706 on November 14, 2013, joined by seven original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the last recorded action [S1][S5].

Ten senators cosponsored the bill — 9 Democrats and 1 Independent — but no Republican signed on and the Finance Committee took no action during the 113th Congress, which ended January 3, 2015 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that profit from classifying employees as independent contractors, and incumbent members of Congress who faced no vote, were better off because the bill never advanced. Misclassified workers kept none of the protections or notices the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Contractor-reliant businesses; the bill died unseen

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled original cosponsors

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did

against.what_they_did: Took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — after the bill was referred on November 14, 2013

against.what_they_did: Had a strong financial stake in keeping the 1978 ban on Treasury classification guidance in place, which the bill would have repealed

sides.party_line_note: All 11 senators attached to the bill were Democrats or the chamber's Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced far enough for a recorded vote.

industries.industry: Staffing firms and businesses built on independent-contractor labor
industries.note: These businesses save roughly the cost of payroll taxes, unemployment insurance, and benefits by treating workers as contractors. The bill would let Treasury clarify status, require contractor notices, and end reduced penalties where there is no reasonable basis, raising their labor costs [S2][S3].

A dedicated provision says compliance-driven instructions cannot count toward broker employee status, making it easier to keep registered representatives off employee status, and it applies retroactively to services after 1997 [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Law-abiding employers who classify workers correctly
industries.note: Misclassification lets competitors undercut them on price; clearer rules and stronger penalties would level the competitive field, which the bill's own findings describe as an inequity [S2][S3].
Misclassification contributes to the federal and state tax gap; clearer classification and enforcement would recover uncollected employment taxes that otherwise fall on compliant taxpayers [S2].
